title: KOSPI Hits 6 Month Low on $3.6B Foreign Selloff

tickers.name: SK hynix Inc. American Depositary Shares

summary:
South Korea's main equity index ended Thursday trading down 7.6%, marking a six-month low after the semiconductor sector plummeted 12% and triggered market-wide circuit breakers. Foreign investors drove the rout, offloading $3.6B in Korean equities, including $1.1B in Samsung and $830M in SK Hynix. The turmoil extended to the KOSDAQ, which also triggered a trading halt during the session after the index fell past the 8% threshold, causing all equity and program trading to freeze for 20 minutes.

The KOSPI has fallen 21% over the last seven trading sessions, the steepest decline for the index since the pandemic crash in March 2020, and now sits 40% below its June 19 record peak. The selloff was fueled by hot US inflation data that raised Federal Reserve rate hike fears and concerns over a global memory-chip oversupply starting in 2029. South Korean regulators called an emergency meeting to discuss market stability, citing concerns that increased RAM production in China by late 2028 could permanently impair the country's dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix.

selectedTweets.text:
South Korea's stock market is in FREE FALL and the panic surrounding the memory trade is getting completely out of control.

The KOSPI just plunged another 7%, bringing its decline to roughly 40% from its June highs. Samsung and SK Hynix are getting absolutely destroyed, and the selling pressure is spreading across the entire AI infrastructure trade. I went on Making Money with @cvpayne today to talk about the memory selloff and why I believe investors are losing sight of what's actually happening in this industry.

And now we're getting ANOTHER warning out of South Korea. A new column published by Maeil Business Newspaper is raising concerns that the global memory industry could face oversupply beginning in 2029 as new manufacturing capacity starts coming online. The argument is that South Korea has become increasingly dependent on Samsung and SK Hynix, and that the country has roughly two to three years to develop other growth industries before the memory cycle potentially reverses. Now, I think this is something investors should absolutely pay attention to but here's where I disagree with the panic.

We're talking about a potential oversupply problem in 2029 while the industry is still struggling to meet demand TODAY. Memory manufacturers are already dealing with capacity constraints, AI customers are securing long term supply agreements, and demand for HBM continues to grow as Nvidia $NVDA and other AI chipmakers push toward increasingly memory intensive systems. And people need to understand that building additional manufacturing capacity doesn't automatically mean we're going to have an oversupply problem. These fabs take years to construct, equipment needs to be installed, production yields need to improve, and manufacturers still have to qualify their products with customers. Not to mention, HBM manufacturing is substantially more complicated than traditional DRAM, and not all additional memory capacity can immediately be used to produce the most advanced AI memory products.

Now, could we eventually see oversupply in 2029? ABSOLUTELY. Memory is a cyclical industry and I've never argued that these companies will enjoy record pricing and margins forever. But there's a massive difference between acknowledging that possibility and acting like the memory cycle is already over. I still believe the fundamentals of the memory trade remain incredibly strong, especially for companies positioned to benefit from HBM and the broader AI infrastructure buildout. This selloff in memory stocks makes absolutely NO sense to me.

$MU, $SNDK, Samsung and SK Hynix are getting hit after China's CXMT announced progress on its new 4F² DRAM architecture, with plans to introduce DDR5 server memory using the technology by the end of 2026. For those unfamiliar, this technology is designed to pack more memory cells into the same amount of space, potentially improving chip density and manufacturing efficiency.

Now, I want to make something clear. CXMT is absolutely becoming a legitimate competitor because acording to TrendForce, CXMT has already captured roughly 9.5% of global DRAM revenue, up from 7.6% the previous quarter, making it the fourth largest DRAM manufacturer globally. The company is also expanding aggressively, with new manufacturing facilities in Shanghai and Hefei targeting more than 600,000 wafers per month, potentially doubling its manufacturing capacity. On top of that, CXMT has reportedly started mass production of its G5 DRAM platform and LPDDR6 memory, while its new 4F² architecture could make memory production even more efficient.

But here's why I think the market is getting WAY ahead of itself. First, announcing a new memory architecture and successfully manufacturing it at scale are two completely different things. CXMT still needs to prove it can deliver competitive yields, pricing, reliability, and production volumes. Second, we're currently dealing with an enormous memory supply shortage, particularly as hyperscalers continue increasing AI infrastructure spending. Even if CXMT successfully doubles its capacity, that doesn't automatically mean the industry becomes oversupplied. Demand for memory is expected to grow substantially over the next several years, and we're already seeing manufacturers secure longer term supply agreements with customers.

Third, this announcement is primarily focused on conventional DDR5 server memory, NOT HBM. That's an important distinction because HBM is becoming one of the most valuable parts of the memory industry, with Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix benefiting from enormous AI demand. And SanDisk primarily manufactures NAND flash memory, not DRAM. So selling $SNDK specifically because of a DDR5 technology announcement seems even more questionable. Now, that doesn't mean CXMT won't eventually put pressure on conventional DRAM prices. Increased Chinese manufacturing capacity is absolutely something investors should monitor, especially over the longer term but I think investors are confusing a legitimate long term competitive threat with an immediate change in industry fundamentals. Nothing about today's announcement suddenly creates millions of additional memory chips, eliminates existing supply shortages, or changes the amount of memory needed to power AI infrastructure. I've been saying this for months. The amount of memory we're going to need over the next decade is INSANE. selectedTweets.text:
🦔Korea is the purest AI bet in the world, so it falls first and hardest. Two chip companies make up more than half the market, retail investors loaded up on leveraged funds tied to both, and the index doubled in six months on memory prices that had already quadrupled. Local reports blamed Wednesday’s hot US inflation report and CoreWeave’s debt for today’s leg down.

I don’t think this is the bottom. Samsung just posted a record quarter and its stock keeps sinking, so investors are pricing in where memory prices go next year, and with China’s CXMT adding capacity and US borrowing costs climbing, buyers have little reason to rush back in. 

My guess is Seoul steps in soon with a stabilization fund or limits on short selling like it did in 2020, which might stop the bleeding for a few days but won’t change where memory prices are headed. Korean investors also put $69 billion into US stocks over the past year, and if losses at home force sales, some of that money comes out of Nvidia and Micron.

Hedgie🤗
